questions.title: What does it mean for a federal court to 'certify' a question to a state supreme court?
questions.question_body: I'm reading the end of the opinion where the Plaintiffs ask the 5th Circuit to certify the issues to the Louisiana Supreme Court. I thought that in diversity cases, the federal court just applies state law as it is written. Why would they ask the state court for a ruling, and what is the 'compelling reason' the court is looking for to justify doing so?

questions.title: How can 'strict adherence' to a statute justify ignoring a requirement like a signature?
questions.question_body: The court cites multiple cases saying Louisiana requires 'strict adherence' to the cancellation statute and that 'any defect' results in an ineffective cancellation. However, when discussing the missing signature, the court says 'strict adherence' is not an invitation for courts to add to the procedures. This feels contradictory—if the goal is strict adherence to protect the insured, why isn't the lack of a signature considered a 'defect'?

questions.title: Can an automated API call satisfy a statutory requirement for the 'receipt' of a notice?
questions.question_body: In this case, the Plaintiffs argue that 'receipt' requires physical possession. The court cites Black's Law Dictionary, which mentions 'taking physical possession,' but then concludes that a computer 'web service' acting as a 'listener' satisfies the requirement. I'm confused about the legal reasoning here: how does a digital trigger count as 'possession' or 'receipt' in a legal sense if no human ever touched the document?

questions.title: Why was the district court's 'private carrier' interpretation considered 'imaginative and unconventional'?
questions.question_body: The district court held that the APAC employee who delivered the notices fit the definition of a 'private carrier.' The 5th Circuit dismissed this reasoning as 'imaginative.' I don't understand the legal distinction here. If a person is hired to carry a document from point A to point B, aren't they effectively a private carrier? What is the court implying is the correct definition of a 'private carrier'?

questions.title: Does the term 'certifying' in a statute inherently imply a signature requirement?
questions.question_body: The core of the dispute is whether the word 'certifying' in La. Rev. Stat. § 9:3550(G)(3)(a) requires a signature. The court finds that because the statute doesn't explicitly say 'signed,' a signature isn't required. Is this a general rule of statutory interpretation (that implied requirements are ignored if not explicit), or is this specific to insurance law?
